summary: llmcord is a single-file Discord bot with exactly one LLM call: the streamed chat.completions request in on_message that writes the bot's reply into a Discord embed, built from a per-provider AsyncOpenAI client whose base_url and model come from config.yaml. Its product promise is that any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works (OpenAI, OpenRouter, xAI, Google, Azure, and local LM Studio / Ollama / vLLM), so the migration puts the vendored Router runtime under that client instead of pointing it at Router: with RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY set, a configured model that is a Router catalog id (the shipped default, openai/gpt-5.5) is translated to Router's /v1/responses and streamed back as chat chunks, while anything Router cannot serve - ollama/llama4, the OpenRouter "~anthropic/..." ids, OpenRouter's own web_search tool, Azure deployments - goes to its provider exactly as before, and nothing changes at all until the key is set. The reply path was driven end to end against the local simulator and against real Router (200, served by openai, snarky system prompt and streamed edits intact), and the Dockerfile now copies the runtime so the documented container deploy actually routes.
reviewed: One call, one client, one global model: I read the whole 347-line module as the reply path a human waits on - how the reply chain is rebuilt from Discord on every message (up to 25 messages, 100k characters, 5 images, resent in full each turn), how the model is chosen (one process-wide curr_model switched by an admin slash command), what happens when a provider fails (the exception is logged and the user is left with a half-written orange embed), and what the request costs at the shipped default (gpt-5.5, $5/$30 per 1M - the priciest OpenAI id in the catalog). That shape made the improvements write themselves: the request's cacheable prefix was being destroyed by a clock in the system prompt, there was no timeout and no cross-vendor failover, the model choice is global rather than per channel or per message, and the chain is capped in characters when Router can count tokens for free. I did not propose anything around tool use, structured output or state: llmcord uses none, Router keeps no state, and the reply chain already lives in Discord.

items.title: Route the Discord reply call through Router
items.summary: The per-message AsyncOpenAI client is wrapped with the vendored runtime, so the streamed reply goes to Router's /v1/responses when RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set.
items.gains: The bot's only LLM call reaches Router with one key: the catalog's models on both API surfaces, per-request spend records labelled llmcord.py:on_message, and a provider retry if Router refuses before generating. Chat Completions keeps working even though Router serves no /v1/chat/completions endpoint.
items.price: no change: the same model at the same catalog price (gpt-5.5 $5/$30 per 1M), served at the account's default tier.
items.why: llmcord's value is that it speaks Chat Completions to anything, including local servers, and the reply is streamed into a Discord embed chunk by chunk. Pointing the client at Router would 404 on chat.completions, and porting the loop to Responses would fork the streaming code for providers that have no Responses API. The runtime routes per request instead: catalog models go to Router, everything else stays with its provider, and models the runtime cannot translate (OpenRouter's web_search tool) fall back untouched. The Dockerfile copied only llmcord.py, so the image needed router_runtime.py too or the container would silently never route.

check --run tests/route_check.py: 1 valid /v1/responses, feature=llmcord.py:on_message; check --all: 1 of 1 call ROUTES

items.title: A route check that drives the reply path
items.summary: New tests/route_check.py calls the real on_message with stub Discord objects, so the streamed reply is exercised against router-sim or real Router rather than only imported.
items.gains: Route truth and behaviour are checked together: the chunk loop, the embed edits, the message chain and the config's reasoning_effort/verbosity all run against Router in one command. The project's own test command (compileall + import) is unchanged.
items.price: one small generation per run; about $0.01 at gpt-5.5 when run live.
items.why: The repository has no test suite, so without a harness nothing proves the call reaches Router - the scanner can only see that the client is wrapped. The repo's .gitignore is a whitelist, so tests/*.py had to be listed in it.

evidence.detail: exit 0, 1 request to Router, reply text non-empty

items.title: Local and non-catalog providers stay put
items.summary: Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, Azure, Gemini and the OpenRouter "~anthropic/..." ids keep going to their own endpoints, because Router serves only catalog ids on its own hosts.
items.gains: llmcord still works offline and with every provider its README advertises; an operator running ollama/llama4 sees no change whether or not a Router key is set.
items.why: This is deliberate, not a gap. The runtime routes a request only when its host is OpenAI's and its model resolves to a catalog id; an OpenRouter id like ~anthropic/claude-opus-latest does not, and the config's openrouter:web_search tool is untranslatable, so those requests go to OpenRouter unchanged. Unlocking another vendor's host (runtime unlock_hosts) would route e.g. x-ai/grok-4.7 to Router, but it would also silently drop provider-specific extra_body fields that only that vendor understands, so it needs an operator's decision rather than a default.

evidence.detail: runtime plan_request: catalog-id + OpenAI host required; config.yaml's non-OpenAI providers and ids do not match

items.title: Make the reply prompt prefix cacheable
items.summary: Send the system prompt's {date}/{time} lines after the conversation instead of in front of it, and set prompt_cache_key for this feature, so repeated reply chains hit the prompt cache.
items.gains: Every follow-up in a reply chain resends the whole chain, and today the request's first bytes are a clock that changes every second, so no two requests share a prefix and prompt caching never pays. With the clock moved last and a cache key set, the stable system prompt plus the earlier turns become a cacheable prefix: measured -50% on a 9k-token gpt-4o-mini prompt and -90% on Claude via Responses (ROUTER.md 6.3). At the shipped default, cached input is $0.50 instead of $5.00 per 1M tokens.
items.loses: The model reads the date and time after the conversation rather than before it - the same information in a different position, so answers can differ slightly.
items.price: A cached read costs the catalog's cache_read_input (gpt-5.5 $0.50 vs $5.00 per 1M input); caching pays only above the provider's ~1,024-token minimum, so short one-off DMs are unaffected either way.
items.why: This is the single largest cost lever in the app, because llmcord's conversation model is 'resend the entire reply chain every turn' and its prompts are large by design (25 messages, up to 100k characters, images). prompt_cache_key is set in router.policy.json, so it is added only to Router-bound requests and the provider path keeps exactly the body the code built. The split is conservative: only lines containing {date} or {time} move, and a system prompt without those placeholders is sent exactly as before.

evidence.detail: check --run tests/route_check.py --live on the branch: 200 /v1/responses, reply intact
planner dump of the real on_message body: input = [stable system, user, clock system] and prompt_cache_key=llmcord.py:on_message from the policy
compileall + import llmcord
catalog: gpt-5.5 in $5, cache-read $0.50 per 1M; measured cache behaviour from ROUTER.md 6.3, not re-measured for gpt-5.5

items.title: Fall back to another vendor when OpenAI refuses
items.summary: router.policy.json sends the reply as models [gpt-5.5, gpt-5.2, claude-sonnet-5], so a pre-stream failure is answered by the next candidate instead of logging an exception.
items.gains: Today a provider 5xx, a 429 or a refused model ends as 'Error while generating response' in the log and a half-written orange embed for whoever is waiting in Discord. A models list lets Router try the next candidate - including a different vendor - before the first streamed event, which is exactly when provider outages show up.
items.loses: Another model may answer, so answers will differ; the least capable candidate limits what the request may use; and no fallback happens once the stream has started, so a mid-stream failure still fails.
items.price: The serving candidate's price when it serves (gpt-5.2 $1.75/$14, claude-sonnet-5 $2/$10 vs gpt-5.5 $5/$30). Flex is not requested with a list and Router ignored allow_flex_tier alongside one (ROUTER.md 6.2); a plain candidate list was still served at Flex in 3 of 3 measured calls, which was not re-measured for gpt-5.5.
items.why: A Discord bot that answers with a different model is far better than one that answers with nothing, and this is the failure the app currently handles worst - it has no retry at all. The capability guard drops candidates that cannot serve the request (images, tools), and keeping it in the policy means the provider fallback path never sees a Router-only field.

evidence.detail: check --run tests/route_check.py --live on the branch: 200 /v1/responses with a models list, served by the primary (provider=openai)
check --run: 1 valid Router request; runtime log confirms no candidate dropped by the capability guard

items.title: Cap a stalled provider at 60 seconds
items.summary: provider_timeout 60 for this feature, so a provider that stops streaming fails in a minute instead of hanging on the OpenAI SDK's 600s default.
items.gains: Bounded failure on a path a human is watching: Discord stops showing the bot as typing after a minute of silence instead of up to ten, and the slot in the bot's event loop is released. 60s is idle time between streamed events, which is an order of magnitude above a healthy stream.
items.loses: A generation that genuinely goes quiet for more than 60 seconds now ends in a 504 and a partial reply instead of eventually completing.
items.price: no change; a timed-out attempt is still billed for what it produced.
items.why: The app sets no timeout anywhere and swallows the exception, so a stalled provider is invisible except as a bot that never answers. If this is applied together with i1, both keys belong in the one llmcord.py:on_message entry of router.policy.json followed by `router-migrate policy`.

evidence.detail: check --run tests/route_check.py on the branch: 1 valid /v1/responses with the compiled policy loaded
compileall + import llmcord (policy-only change)

items.title: Default to a cheaper chat model
items.summary: Ship config.yaml with gpt-5.1 or gpt-5.6-luna as the first model instead of gpt-5.5, the most expensive OpenAI id in the catalog.
items.gains: The default is what most operators run, and gpt-5.5 is $5/$30 per 1M with reasoning_effort: high on a snarky brief-answer chat bot. gpt-5.1 is $1.25/$10 (4x cheaper in, 3x out), gpt-5.6-luna is $0.20/$1.20 (25x in, 25x out); both are Flex-eligible and still vision models, so images keep working. A 5k-token chain with a 300-token reply costs about $0.034 at gpt-5.5, $0.009 at gpt-5.1, $0.0014 at gpt-5.6-luna.
items.loses: answers will differ - a smaller model is worse at long reply chains and at the config's high reasoning effort, and this is a taste call about the bot's voice that an operator should make, not a safe default swap.
items.price: gpt-5.1 $1.25/$10, gpt-5.6-luna $0.20/$1.20 vs gpt-5.5 $5/$30 per 1M (catalog, live).
items.why: I did not build this: nothing offline measures reply quality, the model is one line of the operator's own config, and the /model command already lets an admin switch at runtime. Worth a human picking a number knowing the multiples.

evidence.detail: router-migrate levers gpt-5.5 and the live catalog: same-family rows gpt-5.4 $2.5/$15, gpt-5.2 $1.75/$14, gpt-5.1 $1.25/$10, gpt-5.6-luna $0.20/$1.20

items.title: Label spend per Discord server
items.summary: Add metadata (guild id, channel id, the requesting user) to Router-bound requests so spend can be read per server instead of as one bucket.
items.gains: Every request today carries one label, llmcord.py:on_message, so Router's spend views cannot say which server or which person is spending. Responses takes up to 16 short labels per request, and `user` and `product` are special keys for Ramp spend management: with them, a bot shared across servers can be charged back, rate-limited by cost, or have a noisy channel found in one query.
items.loses: Discord ids reach Router's usage records, which is a (small) new data flow about who is talking to the bot; and the labels have to be added only when Router is active, since a non-OpenAI provider would reject unknown body fields.
items.why: This is the observability half of 'one key for all traffic' and it is cheap - a dict built from new_msg. It needs code rather than router.policy.json, because policy metadata is static per feature while the useful labels are per request, and it must be conditional on RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY so the Ollama path keeps a clean body.

evidence.detail: proposal only; ROUTER.md 6.4 - Responses stores up to 16 labels, Messages forwards only user_id

items.title: Budget the chain in tokens, not characters
items.summary: Trim the reply chain with Router's free /v1/messages/count_tokens instead of guessing with max_text characters and max_messages.
items.gains: The caps are 25 messages, 100,000 characters each and 5 images, so a long thread can send tens of thousands of tokens and cost real money per reply at gpt-5.5 ($5 per 1M input) with no way for the operator to bound it. count_tokens is free on Router and exact for Anthropic-served models, so the bot could drop the oldest turns until the request fits a token budget and say so in the warning embed it already renders ('Only using last N messages').
items.loses: An extra round trip (free, but latency) before each reply, and the count is an estimate for models Anthropic does not serve, so the budget needs headroom.
items.price: no change: count_tokens is free; the point is to cap what the generation costs.
items.why: Characters are a poor proxy for tokens across the vendors llmcord supports (and useless for images), and the existing warning machinery means the user-visible half of this is already built. It is a contained change to the chain-building loop, but it changes which messages the model sees, so it deserves a human's eye on the budget number.

evidence.detail: proposal only; ROUTER.md 2 - count_tokens is served and free, with x-router-token-count-source saying exact or estimated

items.title: Pick the model per channel, not per process
items.summary: Replace the single global curr_model and the per-provider base_url/api_key table with a catalog id chosen per channel (and defaulted per server), now that one key serves every vendor.
items.gains: Today one admin's /model switch changes the model for every server, channel and DM the bot is in, and a new vendor means a new provider block and a new key in .env. On Router, 'which vendor' stops being a deployment decision: the config collapses to a list of catalog ids with their parameters, /model becomes a per-channel setting, and a support channel can run claude-sonnet-5 while a joke channel runs gpt-5.6-luna at 1/25th the input price. It also makes i4 unnecessary - operators pick per use, not once.
items.loses: A real redesign of config.yaml and the /model command, including a compatibility path for the provider blocks that local servers (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM) still need, so existing configs keep working; and per-channel state is new state the bot has to keep somewhere.
items.price: no change by itself; it is what makes cheap-model-per-use possible.
items.why: This is the change I would make first if I were starting llmcord on Router today. The provider table exists because each vendor needed its own base URL and key; with one gateway and one key, the remaining real choice is the model, and the app's own UI (a /model autocomplete over config['models']) is already the right surface for it. Worth a conversation about where per-channel state lives before anyone writes it.

evidence.detail: proposal only; the live catalog serves 90+ ids across 6 vendors on both surfaces with one key

items.title: Speak Responses natively for Router models
items.summary: Give the reply path a second branch that calls /v1/responses directly when the chosen model is a catalog id, keeping chat.completions for everything else.
items.gains: Every Router lever becomes a per-request decision in the code instead of a policy entry keyed by a stack frame: a cache key per conversation, a fallback list chosen for the model in use, fallback_timeout and timeout_before_headers for a user who is watching a stream, Flex on or off per channel, reasoning summaries and text.verbosity, and Responses' own web_search (measured $0.011 a search on gpt-4o-mini) instead of OpenRouter's vendor-specific tool. It also drops the translation layer out of the request path.
items.loses: A second streaming loop to maintain - Responses' events are not chat chunks - and the vendored runtime's automatic provider fallback no longer covers that branch, so the app owns 'Router is down' itself. Local servers and OpenRouter keep the old path, so the file grows a fork.
items.price: no change to model prices; it is the levers, not the rates.
items.why: This is the honest end state of a Router-native llmcord, but it is only worth it after i1-i3 prove the levers matter for this app, and it trades llmcord's single simple loop for two. Proposing it rather than building it.

evidence.detail: proposal only; ROUTER.md 5, 6.1-6.7 - every Router-only field is Responses-only

items.title: Flex pricing or predictable reply latency
items.summary: The account's Flex default halves cost on Flex-eligible OpenAI models but can add seconds to a reply a human is watching; the app can pin either.
items.gains: Keeping Flex (the measured account default, and what the bot gets today) was exactly -50% on gpt-5.4-mini for identical prompts; on gpt-5.5 at $5/$30 that is the largest single price lever after caching. Pinning service_tier default instead removes Flex's tail: Flex latency matched standard in a 5-call sample, but one gpt-5-nano Flex call took 61 seconds, and a streamed Flex attempt is documented to wait up to 25 seconds before falling back to the same model at standard.
items.loses: Whichever one you do not pick: cost or the tail of the wait.
items.price: Flex: -50% measured on gpt-5.4-mini, unmeasured on other models. Standard: full catalog price.
items.why: A Discord bot streams into a message everyone in the channel can see, so a 25-second dead start is very visible - but so is a bill. The lever is one line (service_tier: "default" or allow_flex_tier in the feature's policy entry); which way to set it is a product call about this deployment, and it interacts with i2, since Router ignores Flex alongside a fallback list.

evidence.detail: ROUTER.md 6.1: -50% on gpt-5.4-mini (n=5 per arm); Flex default on for the test account; one 61s Flex call observed

items.title: Failures are invisible to the person waiting
items.summary: on_message catches every exception from the generation and only logs it, so a Router 504, a 429 or an outage shows up in Discord as silence or a half-written orange embed.
items.gains: Reporting the failure in the reply the bot has already posted - it has an embed, a colour convention and a warnings field - would turn 'the bot is broken' into 'try again'. It is a few lines in the existing except branch and needs no Router feature.
items.why: Not a Router change, but it is the other half of i2 and i3: both of those make failure faster and rarer, and neither makes it legible. Worth doing by whoever picks up i3.

evidence.detail: llmcord.py: `except Exception: logging.exception(...)` around the whole stream loop
